en: The smooth spear at his forearm
He seized in his right hand.
Delighted to see the fox,
Never blinking his fixed gaze,
He rode unerringly on!
Taking the path along the slope,
He drew within sight of it,
Into the dust raised by the fox
He plunged.
On the hollow of the pass,
On the level stretch of fescue,
Driving his steed at speed,
Just as he reached the fox,
When winged Kökchebich
Was about to pass alongside,
“God, grant me the cunning one!” he said,
And raised his smooth spear.
The fox urged itself and darted off.
Into caragana, bushes and thick forest,
As the fox fled to enter,
Your leopard champion Syrgak
Struck it once from the side.
Its flank-fur twisted;
Its back broke apart.
In a sign of joy,
Almambet, born a champion,
Came behind him rejoicing.
“My dear Syrgak!” he said,
Tears streaming in ten courses.
“We have slain the fox on the plain!
My dear Syrgak,
Not only my herds and treasures—
For a champion youth like you,
May my own head be a sacrifice!”
Springing down from his horse,
Azizkan's Almambet
Ran up to the fox.
The black steel Narkesken
He drew from its sheath,
And cut it into six pieces,
Drenching the fox in blood.
Caragana branches and masses of rocks—
From among those rocks,
A rawhide bag like a resting camel,
Azizkan's Almambet
Before brave Syrgak
Brought, carrying it aloft.
When he cut it open and looked,
For the fearsome warrior Kongurbay
It was a coat laid ready,
When he came to the watch-post,
A coat for him to wear.
Vowing a sheep to Khorasan,
Offering a prayer to Bahauddin,
Vowing a horse with moon-white hooves,
Almambet stood rejoicing.
The rawhide bag like a resting camel
He slashed open,
And Kongurbay's disguise coat
Almambet took and put on.
When he had put on the coat,
Almambet stood resplendent.
Brave Syrgak watched,
Marveling at Almambet.
Gold gleamed from ring after ring;
A coral stone as large as a leather flask
Shone upon his head.
Seen from outside,
A cotton sash and broad boots—
If you looked at his appearance,
Kongurbay, khan of the monks,
Your Almambet had now become that very man.
The smoking pipe in his hand,
A smooth pipe with a golden crescent—
When viewed from the front,
A fearsome giant big as a hut.
Then, when they had come from vast Talas,
Crying out, moving up and down,
Had she not given it in agitation?
A saddlebag as a gift,
Your heroic sister-in-law Kanykey,
Had she not given it weeping?
“My husband's friend, strap it on if you go to Beijing.
‘My heroic sister-in-law gave this,’ say,
And take it as a gift.
If you go to the Chinese realm's Beijing,
They say the Chinese are like grass;
They say its calamities are many.”
“When he brings trouble upon Beijing,
Let him carry it as a gift,” she thought.
Resourceful Kanykey
Had she not fashioned it?
Kongurbay's Algara,
Ear for ear,
Hoof for hoof,
Making it exactly so,
Had she not fashioned it?
The inner side of the covering
She had bound with fiber.
The outer side, where the hair would lie,
She had covered with black horsehair.
Placing it in the saddlebag and stitching it up,
She entrusted it with instructions.
Poor Kanykey said:
“If you go to Beijing, take it.
Do not think it a burden, my husband's friend;
Strap it to your saddle-strings.
This disguise coat here
I give as a gift; take it.”
Heroic Kanykey,
The disguise coat she had given as a gift—
Your champion Almambet, the leopard,
From Sarala beneath him
Removed the saddle, leaving him bare.
He showed his prowess:
The disguise coat Kanykey had given
He put upon Sarala.
When that disguise coat was on,
The swift Sarala in his disguise,
His Sarala vanished;
Kongurbay's Algara—
He became Algara in appearance.
He tossed his forelock to the sky;
He drove his hooves into the earth;
He rattled his bit.
His tail like strands of silk
He lashed against his hindquarters.
When mounted, Sarala
Tossed and strained like Algara.
Here and there Sarala
Leapt forward and jerked about.
Almambet held his neck high like a rooster;
His sword rang at his side.
When he set off obliquely,
Among the Chinese with red tassels,
He strode splendidly as their mighty one.
Truly, there is no death for you,
Of the Chinese with cap rank-buttons,
Taking the shape of their finest,
Across a pass like a saddle-bow,
He emerged in dust—did you see?
The cunning wild ram was just ahead.
Taking Kongurbay's shape,
Your Almambet came forth deceiving—did you see?
“A dragon lies on the ridge;
Your cunning fox lies there—do you see?
At the place where I stationed the watch,
My champion lies in my fortress;
My duck lies on my lake.
Damn your father's grave, White Ram!
There is no ship on the dark water.
As long as my dear head lives,
There is none to oppose me.
There is no division in the water across the way.
As long as my goshawk head lives,
Keep standing there, cunning ram.
Look now, cunning ram,
My lion standing watch!
For so many years,
As a lookout for me,
You have remained guarding the road.
That I never put you with wild ewes—
That regret belongs to me.
From Karykan's presence,
I shall choose six wild ewes.
In this way, from you
I shall again obtain offspring.”
When it heard this,
Leaving its place, it darted off,
Before your Almambet,
Thinking, “It is my Kongurbay,”
It came racing up.
When it stood broadside,
Your Almambet having tricked the ram,
The brim of the black felt hat—
Have you heard of him?—
Khan Manas's Syrgak,
The short gun in his hand
He aimed and fired once.
Thus he brought down the wild ram.
Young Syrgak, the outstanding warrior,
Laid it low where he fired.
He shot and slaughtered the cunning ram;
The two ate their fill of its meat.
Traveling without pity,
Riding far, sparing no horses,
Over land with no mountain even an ankle-bone high,
With no hollow big enough for a saddlecloth,
Through desert where no dog had passed,
Along a winding road,
He turned his horse's head.
Your poor Almambet
Stood there troubled,
And to Syrgak beside him
Spoke these words:
“On the bluff ahead,
There is a path for a single horse.
The duck has left the lake.
For not arriving two days earlier,
Misfortune falls on Almambet.
Six days ahead,
There is the mighty one called Great Malgun.
He has a club as big as a hut,
And hands with which to wrestle.
The forty monks standing before him
Have their chief at the watchpost.
Before Great Malgun
Lies a sacred text in Chinese.
For the unbeliever Malgun to ride,
They mount him on a gray mule.
That great donkey, swifter than other beasts—
No animal can match its running;
And Malgun upon its back,
None can overcome, however they wrestle him.
If you ask what Malgun is like,
His speech is unlike a human's.
Looking at him from the front,
He has one eye as large as a milk pail.
That is the stronghold of Outer Beijing;
The immeasurably huge Malgun
Is its one-eyed khan.
What times, what nights await us,
Leopard Syrgak, my champion?
For the two of us upon this road,
What days shall there be?
What frightens me, what I fear,
Is that unbeliever Great Malgun.
He spares none who grapple with him;
The meat of a single pig
Will never fill him at one meal.
Consider my words carefully;
Such is what your Alake says.
Beijing of Kakanchyn—
One-eyed Great Malgun
Stands guard over it there.
There, by the mottled-gray saddle and rocky ridge,
His cauldron is boiling.
There on the slope, to the great plane tree,
His mule is tethered.
When I cry the battle name ‘Almambet!’
Get to his mule!
If you reach it, my Syrgak,
Cut off the mule's head.
Listen well to what I say:
‘What has become of Alake?’
Keep your eyes upon me.
If you flee from the Chinese,
I shall know your childishness.
If what is told is true,
On the coming Day of Judgment,
I shall make you a black donkey and ride you!
If I do not tell you, whom shall I tell?
My banner fastened to my spear,
From our little handful of Kyrgyz,
Asked for expressly from Manas,
You are the gift I brought with me.
